overview: The modern Republic of Mali emerged from decolonization in 1960. It is a separate state from the medieval Mali Empire, although its communities preserve and reinterpret much older histories.

periods.title: An independent republic
periods.summary: The former French Sudan became the Republic of Mali after the federation with Senegal broke apart.

periods.title: Rebellion, coup and conflict
periods.summary: A rebellion and coup in 2012 opened a prolonged crisis.

periods.title: Further military takeovers
periods.summary: Military intervention overturned governments in 2020 and 2021.

sections.title: A modern country and its written voices

items.text: This map record represents the modern republic. In 1960, the former French Sudan separated from the short-lived federation with Senegal and became the Republic of Mali. It was not the medieval empire surviving unchanged.

Mali’s recent political history includes a 2012 rebellion and coup, followed by military takeovers in 2020 and 2021. These changes disrupted government without ending the country. Families’ experiences of conflict, displacement and rebuilding belong beside the stories of presidents and soldiers.

A 2016 Bamanankan writing sample is the published title “taamacogo yɛlɛma : mun na hadamaden bɛ jͻ ka taama”, paired with “The Upright Revolution: Or Why Humans Walk Upright”. Malian writer Ismaila Samba Traoré translated Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s story. The Latin-based spelling preserves sounds beyond ordinary English letters.

sections.title: People who keep buildings and books alive

items.text: Djenné’s Great Mosque receives new earthen plaster before the rains. In 2025, communal work took place on 25 May and 12 June. The current building dates to 1907, while the town’s Islamic architectural history is much older.

The plaster called banco mixes earth and water with natural additives, including rice bran, baobab powder and shea butter. The Barey-Ton association of masons organizes the work. A magnificent building needs recipes and regular maintenance, as well as an architect’s original idea.

Men, women, children and visitors join the annual event, which also passes knowledge to younger generations. Conservation becomes a public occasion. Keeping a landmark standing can mean getting together and getting muddy.

During the 2012 occupation of Timbuktu, residents and the heritage organization SAVAMA-DCI rescued most of the city’s ancient manuscripts. Many moved to Bamako. These were family and institutional collections, protected through local effort at considerable risk.

A 2015 conference identified suitable storage boxes and digitization as urgent needs for the rescued manuscripts. Saving a book from destruction is only the beginning: paper also needs careful handling, suitable storage and people who can help future readers use it.

At Markala, Bambara, Bozo, Marka and Somono communities hold festivities with masks, puppets, drums and dancing. Animal figures express social virtues. The celebrations follow harvest rites and lead into a period of fishing, connecting performance with the working year.

Markala’s festivities also create opportunities to discuss quarrels between families and communities. Older people teach young initiates ritual skills. A puppet performance can therefore be entertainment, education and a setting for repairing relationships.

Senufo balafons have wooden keys above gourd resonators. In the form described by UNESCO, delicate membranes made from spider egg-sac material cover holes in the gourds and change the sound. Ingenious musical engineering does not always involve electricity.

Children begin learning on smaller balafons before moving to full-sized instruments with a teacher. Music accompanies work, celebrations and funerals. These Senufo traditions cross borders into neighboring countries, illustrating why a cultural map never fits perfectly inside a political one.

In 2019, Fatoumata Barry taught displaced families in Sévaré through puzzles and playful demonstrations. Ada Diagayété helped compare washing with and without soap. Their stadium shelter had gained sixteen latrines, six showers and six taps: teaching and practical facilities worked together.

ending.text: Mali continues as a country despite prolonged conflict and political upheaval. Its communities maintain social life, education and heritage through these disruptions; a coup is not the disappearance of a people.
